title: The decree
hookLine: all things happen by Allah's knowledge and will, the good and the hard
last: AN ATOM'S WEIGHT OF GOOD WILL BE SEEN.

cards: A bus pulls away just as you reach the stop. A test result comes back. A call with good news, a call with bad.
Moments like those come with a ready-made sentence, and it often starts with if only. A hadith in Sahih Muslim takes that phrase head on.
When something befalls you, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says, don't say if only I had done this. Say: Allah decreed it, and He did what He willed. For if only, he says, opens the door to Satan's work.

teach.b: The word is qadar, decree, measure. In the hadith of Jibril, the list of six ends with it: to believe in the decree, its good and its harm. First, the measure.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! We have created every thing by measure." Nothing is random to Allah's knowledge: what happens is known and willed, the easy days and the hard ones.
Second, what the belief is for.
Another passage says what is coming is already written, so that a person doesn't despair over what slipped away or get carried away by what was given. Qadar steadies both ends, the loss and the win.
That's the work the if only hadith is doing. It doesn't say the bus didn't matter; it says the endless replay doesn't help. Third, what it doesn't mean.
In a hadith in Tirmidhi's collection, a man asks whether to tie his camel or leave it loose and trust Allah. The answer: tie it, and trust. Decree isn't permission to stop trying.
A person still plans, works, takes medicine, ties the camel.

teach.h: DECREE AND CHOICE: AN OPEN QUESTION.
teach.b: Fourth, the open question. How Allah's decree and human choice fit together is an old argument in Islamic theology, and Muslim schools answer it differently; this path meets those theologians soon.
And that completes the six: Allah, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.

how: Belief in qadar, the divine decree, is the sixth article of faith; when something hard happens, Muslims may say that Allah decreed it, and the advice to tie your camel and trust is quoted alongside it.

o: a punishment sent for a sin someone committed in the past
fate that makes human effort pointless, so why try at all
decree: all happens by God's knowledge and will, good and hard

p: the phrase the hadith warns against

s: belief in the decree means there's no point trying
in the hadith of the camel, the answer is: tie it, and trust.
the hadith of Jibril says to believe in the decree, its good and its harm
the sixth article covers the hard as well as the good.
Muslim theologians all answer the decree-and-choice question the same way
it is one of the old arguments of Islamic theology, and schools answer it differently.

games.q: you've ridden a camel to meet the Prophet. do you leave it untied and trust Allah to keep it there?
o: tie it, and don't bother trusting.
games.why: in the hadith in Tirmidhi, the answer is tie it and trust. decree in Islam sits alongside effort, not in place of it.

practice: Find one if only that's been replaying lately, a medium one, not the biggest, and notice the sentence your mind keeps saying about it.
Then gently say what happened, plainly, once: it happened, or, if you pray, Allah decreed it, and He did what He willed. Then notice what's still yours to do next.
If a loss feels too heavy to carry, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Qadar. Decree, measure: belief that all things happen by Allah's knowledge and will, the good and the hard. The sixth article of faith. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: decree, measure; the sixth article of faith.

carryVoice: Your line: all by his decree. The camel still gets tied. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Lo! We have created every thing by measure.
